## What does "per written contract" mean on an additional insured endorsement?

> "Per written contract" looks like it covers everyone your project requirements name. Whether it does depends on whose contract it means, when it was signed and what it says.

Published Oct 30, 2026 by Forsured. COI basics. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/per-written-contract-additional-insured/

![Four checks on a “per written contract” endorsement: Whose contract counts?; Signed before the loss?; Does it require you as additional insured?; Endorsement in hand, not just the certificate?](https://forsured.ai/blog/per-written-contract-additional-insured/hero.png)

### The short version

- "Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires, instead of naming each party on a schedule.
- Some wording only covers parties the named insured contracted with directly. New York's highest court held in 2018 that "with whom you have agreed" by written contract requires that direct contract.
- Courts also look at whether the agreement was in writing, whether it was signed before the loss, and whether it really required additional insured status.
- A certificate doesn't create additional insured status. Get the endorsement, check its wording against your project requirements, and keep the signed contract on file.

"Per written contract" means the policy adds as an additional insured whoever a written contract requires it to add, instead of naming each party on a schedule. It's convenient. One endorsement covers every owner and GC a contractor works for. But it only covers you if your situation fits the endorsement's exact words, and those words differ more than most people expect.

As IA Magazine put it, "There is no such thing as a blanket additional insured endorsement." There are many, and they don't all do the same thing.

### Whose contract counts

The biggest question is whether the endorsement covers only parties the named insured contracted with directly.

New York's Court of Appeals answered it for one common wording in 2018. In Gilbane Building Co./TDX Construction Corp. v. St. Paul Fire and Marine Insurance Co., a construction manager on a Manhattan hospital project required each prime contractor to name it as an additional insured. One prime contractor's policy covered any party "with whom you have agreed to add as an additional insured by written contract." The construction manager had no contract of its own with that prime contractor. The court ruled 5-2 that "with" meant the written contract had to be with the additional insured, so the construction manager wasn't covered.

Other wording reaches further. IA Magazine notes that ISO's CG 20 33 requires privity of contract, while CG 20 38 can extend status to parties the contract requires, further up the chain. Courts in other states have split on similar language, IRMI reports, so the same words can mean different things in different places.

### When it was signed, and what it says

Wording that requires a written agreement can raise more questions:

- **Is it in writing?** Some courts have accepted letters and other written agreements that weren't formal contracts. Others read the requirement strictly.
- **Was it signed in time?** Some endorsements require the agreement to be executed before the loss. IRMI notes courts apply that strictly.
- **Does it actually require additional insured status?** A contract with a blank or vague insurance section can leave you off the policy.

These fights are still live. In a lawsuit filed in federal court in New York and reported by Insurance Business in July, Berkley alleges Trisura refused to defend a project owner under an endorsement whose schedule read "Per Written Contract." Part of the dispute, as reported, is whether a purchase order's insurance exhibit counts as a written contract. The allegations haven't been decided.

### What to check on a contractor COI

1. Get the endorsement, not just the certificate. As Jones Day noted, additional insured status is created only by an endorsement the insurer issues.
2. Read the wording. Look for "with whom," "such person or organization," and any execution or timing requirement.
3. Check it covers every party your project requirements name, including owners and others who don't contract with that contractor directly.
4. Keep the signed contract, with its insurance requirements, on file next to the endorsement.
5. Recheck at renewal, when forms can change.

A blanket endorsement is only as good as the contract behind it. Forsured checks each contractor COI and its endorsements against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

### Common questions

#### What is a blanket additional insured endorsement?

An endorsement that grants additional insured status to any party a written contract requires, instead of listing each party by name. The exact wording varies by form and carrier, so two "blanket" endorsements can cover very different parties.

#### Does a per written contract endorsement cover an owner or GC with no direct contract with the insured?

It depends on the wording. In Gilbane Building Co./TDX Construction Corp. v. St. Paul Fire and Marine (2018), New York's Court of Appeals held that an endorsement covering parties "with whom you have agreed" by written contract required a direct contract between the named insured and the additional insured. Other forms, such as ISO's CG 20 38, extend status to parties further up the contract chain.

#### Is a certificate of insurance enough to prove additional insured status?

No. A certificate summarizes coverage. Additional insured status comes from an endorsement issued by the insurer, and for blanket wording, from a written contract that meets the endorsement's terms.

## Can parametric insurance cover weather delays on a construction project?

> Builder's risk pays when weather damages the work. It doesn't pay when weather stops the work. A panel at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference made the case for closing that gap.

Published Oct 29, 2026 by Forsured. Industry news. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/parametric-builders-risk-weather-gap/

![50%: How much a day below 40°F can cut the strength of poured concrete](https://forsured.ai/blog/parametric-builders-risk-weather-gap/hero.png)

### The short version

- Yes. Parametric policies pay a set amount when a measured trigger is hit, such as a cold, heat, wind, rain or snow threshold, so they can cover weather that halts work without damaging it.
- Traditional builder's risk covers physical damage only, so lost days, overtime and schedule pressure from weather usually fall on the contractor.
- Panelists at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference said cover can be tailored to specific operations, such as cold only on concrete pour days or wind only on crane days.
- Payouts can be used for any purpose, such as funding overtime after a delay.

Yes, it can. Builder's risk insurance pays when weather damages the work. It doesn't pay when weather stops the work. Parametric insurance fills that gap by paying a set amount when a measured trigger is hit at the site, such as a temperature, wind speed or rainfall threshold, whether or not anything was damaged.

That was the case a panel made on Tuesday at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor, as reported by Business Insurance.

### The gap builder's risk leaves

Weather stops work long before it breaks anything. Rose Hall, founder of construction risk advisory firm RH Business Ventures, said a day below 40 degrees could cut poured concrete's strength by 50%, and winds above 20 mph can make some crane operations unsafe. Neither shows up as a builder's risk claim.

"Contractors are just absorbing (non-covered weather losses), mostly silently," Hall said.

The panel also pointed to the human cost. Heat-related worker fatalities have risen, and builders often feel pressure to keep working through extreme conditions to stay on schedule.

### Cover the days that stop your work

Parametric cover doesn't have to insure every storm. Gary Kaplan, former president of construction at AXA XL, put it this way: "The goal is not to cover every weather event. It is to cover the specific events that stop your specific operations at your specific location."

That means a policy can be shaped around the job:

- Cold, but only on concrete pour days.
- Wind, but only on crane days.
- Payouts that can be used for anything, such as overtime to recover a delay.

Chris Smith, a senior director at the Baldwin Group, said larger builders could use it across a portfolio, and captive owners could use a payout to fund the captive's deductible after a catastrophic event. "To me, this is schedule guardianship," he said.

### A better weather number for the bid

Contractors usually set weather allowances in bids from rough estimates. Hall noted that a 10-year average can hide large swings from one year to the next. Kaplan proposed a "zero-weather-day bid," built on site-specific weather estimates, that could give a bidder an edge.

### What it means for project requirements

If parametric cover starts showing up in project requirements, it becomes one more line to verify, with its own triggers, limits and named site. As with every coverage, the certificate is only the summary. The policy terms are what pay. Forsured checks each contractor COI against the coverage a project actually requires, for the life of the job.

Forsured reads every contractor COI and endorsement against them, flags each gap with the reason, and keeps checking through renewals until the job is done.

That clarity across the GC, subcontractor, and broker is where we see the real value." -- Stephanie Massei, Milestone Construction

### Common questions

#### Does builder's risk insurance cover weather delays?

Usually not. Traditional builder's risk covers physical loss or damage to the work. Days lost to cold, heat, wind, rain or snow that don't damage anything typically aren't covered, so contractors absorb the cost.

#### What is parametric insurance in construction?

A policy that pays a pre-agreed amount when a measured condition is met at the site, such as temperature below a set point on a pour day or wind above a set speed on a crane day. It pays on the trigger, not on proof of damage, and the payout can be used for any purpose.

#### Can parametric cover help a contractor bid?

Possibly. Contractors usually set weather allowances from rough averages, and a 10-year average can hide large year-to-year swings. A panelist at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference proposed a zero-weather-day bid backed by site-specific weather estimates and parametric cover.

## What does primary and noncontributory mean on a COI?

> It's one of the most common lines in construction insurance requirements, and one of the most commonly missing endorsements on a contractor's policy.

Published Oct 28, 2026 by Forsured. COI basics. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/primary-and-noncontributory/

![Primary and noncontributory, checked. A sample contractor certificate of insurance: General liability $1M / $2M, meets the requirement; Additional insured CG 20 10 / CG 20 37, meets the requirement; Primary and noncontributory CG 20 01, meets the requirement; Umbrella $10M, Not primary wording. CG 20 01 covers the general liability policy only. The umbrella needs its own primary and noncontributory wording.](https://forsured.ai/blog/primary-and-noncontributory/hero.png)

### The short version

- Primary and noncontributory sets the order in which overlapping policies respond: the contractor's policy pays first, and it doesn't ask the additional insured's own policy to share the loss.
- It's created by an endorsement on the contractor's general liability policy, such as ISO's CG 20 01, not by a line on the certificate.
- ISO's CG 20 01 applies only when a written contract requires it, and only to the general liability policy. Umbrella and excess need their own wording.
- On every contractor COI, ask for the endorsement form, check it covers the parties your project requirements name, and check the umbrella too.

Read the insurance section of almost any construction contract and you'll find the same phrase: additional insured coverage "on a primary and noncontributory basis." It's so common it reads like boilerplate. It isn't. It decides whose insurance pays first when a contractor's work causes a loss, and whose loss history takes the hit.

### What it means

IRMI describes primary and noncontributory as a term used in contract insurance requirements to set the order in which multiple policies covering the same loss respond. Split it in two:

- **Primary:** the contractor's policy responds first to a covered claim against the additional insured, before the additional insured's own policy.
- **Noncontributory:** the contractor's policy doesn't ask the additional insured's own insurance to chip in.

Without it, a general liability policy's "other insurance" condition can treat the GC's or owner's own policy as sharing the loss. That's exactly what the contract was written to avoid.

### Where it comes from

Like additional insured status, primary and noncontributory is created by policy wording, not by the certificate. A checked box or a note in the description of operations on an ACORD 25 doesn't change the policy.

In 2013 ISO introduced an optional endorsement for it, CG 20 01, "Primary and Noncontributory, Other Insurance Condition." As Claims Journal explained at the time, it was added because so many construction contracts require additional insured coverage on a primary and noncontributory basis. Many carriers use it or their own version, and some blanket additional insured endorsements build similar wording in.

### The fine print that trips people up

CG 20 01 comes with two conditions. It applies only when the additional insured is a named insured on another policy, and only when a written contract requires the contractor's coverage to be primary and noncontributory. Missing contract language means missing coverage.

It also amends the general liability policy only. If your project requirements call for primary and noncontributory umbrella or excess coverage, the umbrella needs to say so in its own wording. With umbrella rates still rising, it's an easy gap to miss.

### What to check on a contractor COI

1. Confirm the project requirements actually call for primary and noncontributory, and on which policies (general liability, auto, umbrella).
2. Ask for the endorsement, not just the certificate. Note the form number and edition.
3. Check that it covers the parties your requirements name: owner, lender, GC, others.
4. Check the umbrella or excess policy separately when the requirements extend to it.
5. Recheck at renewal. Endorsements change when policies renew, and forms keep evolving. "Evolving insurance endorsements" were the backdrop for Cullen and Dykman's session on additional insured endorsements at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference.

It's one line in the contract and one endorsement on the policy. Forsured checks both on every contractor COI, against each project's requirements, for the life of the job.

Forsured reads every contractor COI and endorsement against them, flags each gap with the reason, and keeps checking through renewals until the job is done.

- Project requirements with exceptions, not one template for every job
- Endorsement review (additional insured, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory), not just the certificate
- A shared workspace where the contractor's broker sees exactly what's missing
- A person on your team approves every result, with a full review history

> "What stood out to us is that Forsured doesn't just organize the paperwork. It helps us understand what meets the project requirements, what needs attention, and what needs to happen next. That clarity across the GC, subcontractor, and broker is where we see the real value." -- Stephanie Massei, Milestone Construction

Free COI risk check: send one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two, and we'll show you every gap we find. https://forsured.ai/#demo

### Common questions

#### What does primary and noncontributory mean?

It means the contractor's insurance responds first to a covered claim against an additional insured (primary), and does not seek to share the loss with the additional insured's own insurance (noncontributory). It protects the GC's or owner's own policy and loss history.

#### Is primary and noncontributory the same as additional insured?

No. Additional insured status puts you on the contractor's policy. Primary and noncontributory decides the order in which that policy and your own policy pay. Construction contracts usually require both, and each comes from its own endorsement wording.

#### Does CG 20 01 apply to the umbrella policy?

No. ISO's CG 20 01 amends the commercial general liability policy only. If your project requirements call for primary and noncontributory umbrella or excess coverage, check the umbrella policy's own wording.

Some of the largest projects represented at CRC still track contractor insurance in spreadsheets and inboxes. Certificates arrive in different formats from different countries, and the people responsible know they can't see the whole picture.

### 5. The words matter

We came in using the general contractor's shorthand for the paperwork. By the end of day 1 we'd switched to "project requirements" and "contractor COIs." The neutral wording works for general contractors, trade contractors and owners alike, and it describes the real job: every contractor, checked against what the project requires.

## Is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage? Why a COI alone isn't enough

> No. A certificate of insurance is evidence that a contractor bought certain policies on the day it was issued, and the form says it confers no rights on you. Proof of coverage lives in the policy and its endorsements, so a contractor COI only works as a starting point for checking them.

Published Oct 27, 2026, updated Nov 13, 2026 by Forsured. COI basics. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/compliance-isnt-coverage/

![A COI on file isn't proof of coverage. A sample contractor certificate of insurance: General liability $1M / $2M, meets the requirement; Auto liability $1M, meets the requirement; Umbrella $5M, Below $10M required; Additional insured Box checked, No endorsement; Workers' comp Statutory, meets the requirement. The certificate says additional insured. The policy has no endorsement that makes it true.](https://forsured.ai/blog/compliance-isnt-coverage/hero.png)

### The short version

- Most courts won't let a certificate holder rely on a certificate that contradicts the policy. A few states, Ohio among them, have gone the other way.
- Exclusions, endorsement wording and aggregate rules never appear on the certificate, and they're where claims get denied.
- Policies change mid-job: a contractor COI that passed in March can fail by July.
- Check every contractor COI against the project's own requirements, get the endorsements, and keep checking for the life of the job.

Every general contractor has a folder of contractor COIs. Most were looked at once, by someone in a hurry, when the contractor was onboarded. That folder feels like proof of coverage. It isn't, and the reasons are written on the certificate itself.

### What is a certificate of insurance, and what does it prove?

A certificate of insurance proves that certain policies existed on the day it was issued, and not much more. [IRMI](https://www.irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions/certificate-of-insurance) defines it as a document giving evidence that certain general types of insurance have been bought, with the coverage types and limits. That's the whole job: evidence, on one date.

The standard ACORD 25 says so on its face. The [2025/12 edition](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2025/12/acord-25-2025-12-liability.pdf) is "issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights upon the certificate holder," and it doesn't amend, extend or alter the coverage of the policies listed. When the certificate and the policy disagree, the policy wins.

### Why isn't a certificate of insurance proof of coverage?

A certificate of insurance isn't proof of coverage because courts mostly treat it the way the form describes itself. [Koley Jessen](https://www.koleyjessen.com/insights/publications/certificates-of-insurance-proceed-with-caution) notes that most courts won't let a certificate holder rely on a certificate whose contents are wrong. [Taft](https://www.taftlaw.com/news-events/law-bulletins/be-careful-with-certificates-of-insurance-on-construction-projects/) points to a minority view: Ohio's Supreme Court in Pedler v. Aetna (1986) held an insurer to the coverage a certificate described. That split is a reason to check, not a reason to rely.

[Risk Management Magazine](https://www.rmmagazine.com/articles/article/2021/10/01/the-limitations-of-certificates-of-insurance) collected the cases that show what goes wrong in practice:

- A policy was canceled for nonpayment after the certificate was issued, the certificate holder wasn't told, and it couldn't claim under the policy.
- A certificate and policy both named an owner as additional insured, but the endorsement covered only the named insured's own work. A different trade caused the fire, so there was no duty to defend.
- A certificate said a company was covered under a roofer's policy. The court found the policy gave no such coverage.

This is general information, not legal advice. How your state treats a certificate is a question for your attorney.

### What can a contractor COI hide?

A contractor COI hides most of what decides a claim. The one-page form summarizes policies that run dozens of pages, and the details that matter most never make it onto the page.

Table: What a contractor COI shows, and what actually decides coverage
| Item | What the certificate shows | What decides coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Additional insured | A checked ADDL INSD box | The endorsement form and its wording |
| Completed operations | Usually nothing | Whether the endorsement covers work after the job |
| Waiver of subrogation | A checked SUBR WVD box | The waiver endorsement |
| Exclusions | Nothing | The policy: height limits, residential work, labor law, EIFS and more |
| Aggregate | A box for policy, project or location | Whether a per project aggregate endorsement is attached |
| Limits | The amounts you asked for | The policy limits, less paid claims |
| Dates | The term on the day it was issued | Any cancellation or change since |

The 2025/12 edition adds a note worth knowing. It says the limits shown include amounts requested by the certificate holder and may not reflect higher policy limits, and that limits may have been reduced by paid claims. A certificate that shows your required limit may show only your required limit.

### Which exclusions never show on a certificate of insurance?

Exclusions never show on a certificate of insurance, and they're where proof of coverage most often falls apart. The coverages grid lists policy types and limits. It doesn't list what the policy carves out. Common construction exclusions include work above a certain height, residential or condo projects, exterior insulation and finish systems (EIFS), and action-over claims under New York's labor law, where an injured worker sues the owner or GC. A roofer with a height exclusion or a framer with a residential exclusion can hand you a clean certificate for exactly the work the policy won't cover.

The only proof of coverage for those risks is the policy itself: the declarations, the forms schedule and the endorsements. On a high-risk trade, ask the broker to confirm in writing that no exclusion applies to your project's scope of work.

### Does a checked additional insured box make you an additional insured?

A checked additional insured box doesn't make you an additional insured. The ACORD 25 says that if the certificate holder is an additional insured, the policy must have additional insured provisions or be endorsed, and that a statement on the certificate doesn't replace the endorsement.

The endorsement's wording matters too. Forms change often, a point Christopher Ruggiero of [Cullen and Dykman](https://www.cullenllp.com/blog/partner-and-construction-litigation-chair-christopher-ruggiero-to-speak-at-the-2026-irmi-construction-risk-conference-crc/) made at IRMI's 2026 Construction Risk Conference: the coverage you negotiate only holds if the endorsement on the policy matches it. Check that additional insured status covers [completed operations](/blog/completed-operations-additional-insured/), and whether it applies only where a [written contract requires it](/blog/per-written-contract-additional-insured/).

### What should you check against your project requirements instead?

Instead of relying on a contractor COI, check it against the project's own requirements and get the documents behind it:

1. Start from the project requirements, not a generic checklist. Each owner, lender and contract writes its own project requirements, with its own limits and wording.
2. [Read each certificate of insurance line by line](/blog/how-to-check-a-contractor-coi/) against those project requirements: coverages, limits, dates, and a named insured that matches the contracting entity.
3. Ask for the endorsements the project requirements depend on, and read the form numbers and wording.
4. Check state rules on workers' comp and anti-indemnity in the [COI requirements for your state](/coi-requirements/), and whether the aggregate must be [per project](/blog/per-project-aggregate-coi/).
5. Track renewals and expirations, because a certificate doesn't tell you when a policy is [canceled](/blog/notice-of-cancellation-coi/).

Forsured checks each contractor COI and its endorsement forms against the requirements set for that project, flags each gap for your team to approve, and keeps checking for the life of the job.

### Why do carriers care how you check contractor COIs?

Carriers care because a weak contractor COI program shows up in a GC's own losses. [WTW](https://www.wtwco.com/en-us/insights/2026/10/insurance-marketplace-realities-2027-construction) says underwriters give favorable consideration to contractors with strong management of the trade partners they hire, and it expects umbrella and excess rates to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027. That's exactly the line where trade contractors trim, and exactly the line a file of unchecked certificates won't catch. [Run a free COI risk check](/#demo) on one project to see what yours would show.

### About Forsured

Forsured reads every contractor COI and endorsement against them, flags each gap with the reason, and keeps checking through renewals until the job is done.

- Project requirements with exceptions, not one template for every job
- Endorsement review (additional insured, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory), not just the certificate
- A shared workspace where the contractor's broker sees exactly what's missing
- A person on your team approves every result, with a full review history

> "What stood out to us is that Forsured doesn't just organize the paperwork. It helps us understand what meets the project requirements, what needs attention, and what needs to happen next. That clarity across the GC, subcontractor, and broker is where we see the real value." -- Stephanie Massei, Milestone Construction

Free COI risk check: send one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two, and we'll show you every gap we find. https://forsured.ai/#demo

### Common questions

#### Is a certificate of insurance proof of coverage?

No. A certificate of insurance is evidence that certain policies were in force when it was issued. The standard ACORD 25 says it's issued as a matter of information only, confers no rights on the certificate holder, and doesn't amend, extend or alter the policies. The policy and its endorsements decide coverage, so ask for them when the contract depends on them.

#### Does being listed on a contractor COI make me an additional insured?

No. Additional insured status comes from an endorsement on the contractor's policy, and the ACORD 25 says a statement on the certificate doesn't replace it. Ask for the endorsement form and check that its wording matches your contract, including ongoing and completed operations, and that it isn't limited to the contractor's own work in a way your contract doesn't allow.

#### Can I sue the insurer if the certificate of insurance was wrong?

Usually not. Most courts hold that a certificate holder can't rely on a certificate that conflicts with the policy, because the form disclaims any rights. A few states, including Ohio under Pedler v. Aetna (1986), have held insurers to what a certificate described. It's general information, not legal advice, so ask your attorney about your state.

#### What can a certificate of insurance hide?

A certificate of insurance can hide exclusions, the exact wording of additional insured and waiver endorsements, whether the aggregate is shared across every job, limits that only match what you requested, and a cancellation that happened after it was issued. None of those show on the one-page form, and each one can decide whether a claim is paid.

#### How often should contractor COIs be checked?

Contractor COIs should be checked at onboarding and again whenever a policy renews, changes or nears expiration. On a long project that means checking continuously rather than once at prequalification, because a certificate is accurate only on the day it was issued and policies can be canceled or reissued with new terms mid-job.

3. [The Limitations of Certificates of Insurance](https://www.rmmagazine.com/articles/article/2021/10/01/the-limitations-of-certificates-of-insurance), Risk Management Magazine, Oct 1, 2021
4. [Be Careful With Certificates Of Insurance On Construction Projects](https://www.taftlaw.com/news-events/law-bulletins/be-careful-with-certificates-of-insurance-on-construction-projects/), Taft, Sep 21, 2011
5. [Certificates of Insurance: Proceed with Caution](https://www.koleyjessen.com/insights/publications/certificates-of-insurance-proceed-with-caution), Koley Jessen, Jan 31, 2023

## 3 takeaways from day 2 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference

> The endorsement decides who's protected, prequalification is a snapshot, and insurance data sitting in PDFs is its own kind of risk.

Published Oct 27, 2026 by Forsured. Event takeaways. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-crc-2026-day-2-takeaways/

![Day 2 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference: The endorsement decides who's protected; Prequalification is a snapshot; PDFs can't be searched](https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-crc-2026-day-2-takeaways/hero.png)

### The short version

- Additional insured coverage only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy matches the project requirements, and endorsement forms keep changing.
- Prequalification checks insurance once. Policies renew, lapse and get re-endorsed mid-project, so compliance has to be checked continuously.
- Contractor COIs stored as PDFs can't be trended, audited or shared with a broker or carrier at renewal.

Day 2 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference is a wrap. Three things we were digging into on Tuesday.

### 1. The endorsement is the contract's last line of defense

Tuesday opened with "Decoding Additional Insured Endorsements for Successful Contractual Risk Transfer," led by Christopher Ruggiero, partner and construction litigation chair at Cullen and Dykman. His preview made a point every GC should hear: as claim costs rise, the indemnity and additional insured coverage you negotiate is harder to secure, because the endorsement forms keep changing.

The coverage you negotiated only holds if the endorsement on the contractor's policy actually matches your project requirements. A checked box on a COI doesn't tell you that. The form number and its wording do.

### 2. Prequalification is a snapshot. Insurance is a moving target.

"The Prequalification Puzzle" was on Tuesday's agenda, and it's a good reminder of how much happens after a contractor clears prequal. A contractor COI that passed in March can be out of compliance by July. Policies renew with new terms, lapse for nonpayment and get re-endorsed mid-project.

Prequalification answers "can this firm do the work?" It was never built to answer "is this firm covered today, for this project?"

### 3. Insurance data you can't search is its own risk

Contractor COIs sitting as PDFs in an inbox can't be trended, audited or shared with your broker or carrier when renewal comes around. "When Data Becomes Risk" was on the afternoon agenda, and that's the version of it we see most: the information exists, but nobody can answer a simple question like "which of our active contractors carry less umbrella than the job requires?"

Structured COI data turns that into a two-minute answer, and it's the same data a carrier wants to see when it asks how you manage the trades you hire.

If you want that answer for one of your own projects, start with one project's requirements and a contractor COI or two.

### Common questions

#### Why do additional insured endorsements matter more than the certificate?

Additional insured status is created by an endorsement on the contractor's policy. The certificate only reports it. If the endorsement form is narrower than the contract requires, for example covering ongoing but not completed operations, the gap stays even though the certificate looks fine.

#### Is prequalification enough to manage contractor insurance risk?

No. Prequalification is a point-in-time review. Contractor policies renew, lapse and change during a project, so insurance compliance needs to be rechecked whenever a policy changes and before it expires.

## IRMI is rewriting its design-build risk and insurance guide

> Design-build moves design responsibility onto the builder's side of the table. Project requirements, and the contractor COIs checked against them, have to keep up.

Published Oct 27, 2026 by Forsured. Industry news. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-design-build-guide-update/

![What design-build changes in COI review: Professional liability; Delegated design scopes; Project-specific programs](https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-design-build-guide-update/hero.png)

### The short version

- IRMI selected brokerage American Global to rewrite its Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide, edited by IRMI's Megan Jolly.
- The update covers progressive design-build, risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability, project-specific coverage and bonding.
- On design-build work, check contractor COIs for professional liability wherever a contractor carries design responsibility, not just general liability.

The International Risk Management Institute (IRMI) has picked American Global, a construction and infrastructure risk and insurance brokerage, to rewrite its long-running Design-Build Risk and Insurance guide. The team includes Caryn Maxfield, Ante Petricevic, François Wasselin and Giovanni Bach, with IRMI's Megan Jolly editing, according to the October 23 announcement.

### What the update covers

The rewrite is meant to catch up with how design-build is delivered today, including progressive design-build. It covers contractual risk allocation, indemnification, limits of liability, professional liability insurance, project-specific coverage and bonding.

### Why it matters for contractor COIs

Design-build shifts design responsibility to the builder's side of the contract. That has a direct effect on what a compliant contractor COI looks like:

- **Professional liability enters the picture.** A design-builder, and any trade contractor doing delegated design on mechanical, electrical, structural steel or curtain wall scopes, may need professional liability that a general liability policy won't provide.
- **Requirements differ by role.** The same project can need different coverage from a designer, a design-builder and a build-only trade contractor. One template for every firm misses that.
- **Project-specific programs change the checklist.** When an owner or contractor buys project-specific coverage, contractor COIs have to be checked against what the program does and doesn't cover.

WTW's 2027 outlook expects contractor's professional liability to run flat to up 5% on annual programs and flat to up 10% on project-specific policies, so the coverage is available. The job is making sure the contractors who need it actually carry it, at the limits the project requires.

IRMI's guides are a standard reference for construction risk teams, and this one is worth reading when it lands.

## How to read a certificate of insurance: checking a contractor COI against your project requirements

> To read a contractor COI, start with your project requirements, then check the ACORD 25 field by field: named insured, insurers, each coverage and limit, policy dates, the additional insured and waiver boxes, and the description. A checked box proves nothing alone. Ask for the endorsement forms behind it.

Published Oct 27, 2026, updated Nov 13, 2026 by Forsured. How-to. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/how-to-check-a-contractor-coi/

![Five checks for every contractor COI: Named insured; Coverages and limits; Policy dates; Endorsements; Certificate holder](https://forsured.ai/blog/how-to-check-a-contractor-coi/hero.png)

### The short version

- The ACORD 25 says it confers no rights on the certificate holder. The policy and its endorsements decide coverage.
- The 2025/12 edition notes that limits shown can include only the amounts the holder requested, and may have been reduced by paid claims.
- Most gaps sit in five places: umbrella limits, completed operations, the aggregate, entity names and expiration dates.
- Send the broker the exact requirement and the exact line that misses it. Specific asks get fixed in days.

Knowing how to read a certificate of insurance is mostly knowing what it can't prove. The certificate summarizes a contractor's coverage on one page. Your job is to hold that summary against the project requirements for this job, line by line, and then ask for the documents behind anything that matters.

### What do you need before you read a certificate of insurance?

Learning how to read a certificate of insurance starts with the contract, not the certificate. Pull the insurance section of the subcontract or the project's insurance requirements exhibit. A contractor COI can only pass or fail against something written down. For this project, note:

- Each required coverage: general liability, auto, workers' compensation and employer's liability, umbrella or excess, and anything trade-specific like professional or pollution liability
- The minimum limit for each, and whether the umbrella must follow form
- Required endorsements: additional insured for ongoing and completed operations, waiver of subrogation, primary and noncontributory
- Who must be named: owner, lender, GC and anyone else the contract lists
- How long completed operations coverage must last after the job, and whether the aggregate must apply per project

Requirements differ by owner, lender and contract, so a template from the last job is a guess, not a standard.

### What does each ACORD 25 field tell you?

The ACORD 25 is the standard liability certificate, published by [ACORD](https://www.acord.org/standards-architecture/acord-forms). The current edition is 2025/12 (the [form as posted by the New York Department of Financial Services](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2025/12/acord-25-2025-12-liability.pdf)). Here's how to read a certificate of insurance on that form, field by field.

Table: ACORD 25 fields and what to check against your project requirements
| ACORD 25 field | What it shows | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| Date | When the certificate was issued | A certificate from last year proves nothing about today |
| Producer | The agent or broker who issued it | Who you'll ask for fixes; not proof of coverage |
| Insured | The contractor's legal name and address | Matches the entity on the contract, not a parent, DBA or sister company |
| Insurers A to F, NAIC # | The carriers behind each policy | Real, named carriers; the NAIC number lets you look them up |
| INSR LTR | Which insurer writes each line | Every required line has a carrier |
| ADDL INSD | Additional insured is claimed on that line | A claim only; ask for the endorsement form |
| SUBR WVD | Waiver of subrogation is claimed | Same: ask for the endorsement |
| Policy number, EFF, EXP | Each policy and its dates | In force for the whole job; note every expiration |
| Limits | Each occurrence, aggregates, products and completed operations | At or above every required limit |
| Gen'l aggregate applies per | Policy, project or location | Per project, if your contract requires it |
| Umbrella or excess | Limit, occurrence or claims-made | Meets the requirement; follow form if required |
| Workers' comp and E.L. | Statutory coverage and employer's liability limits | Covers the states where the work is |
| Description of operations | Free text, often the project and named parties | Names this project and your contract where required |
| Certificate holder | Who asked for the certificate | Your correct legal entity |
| Cancellation | How notice of cancellation works | Notice follows the policy, not the certificate |

Forsured reads the certificate and the endorsement forms attached to each contractor COI, checks them against the requirements set for that project, and flags every line that falls short.

### What doesn't a contractor COI tell you?

A contractor COI on the ACORD 25 doesn't create coverage. The form says it's issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights on the certificate holder, and that it doesn't amend, extend or alter the policies. That's why [a COI alone isn't enough](/blog/compliance-isnt-coverage/).

Three lines on the form are worth knowing by heart:

- **The additional insured note.** If the certificate holder is an additional insured, the policy must have additional insured provisions or be endorsed. A statement on the certificate doesn't replace the endorsement.
- **The limits note.** The 2025/12 edition says the limits shown include amounts requested by the certificate holder and may not reflect policy limits above those requested. It also says limits may have been reduced by paid claims. A certificate that shows your required limit may show only your required limit.
- **The cancellation box.** "Should any of the above described policies be cancelled before the expiration date thereof, notice will be delivered in accordance with the policy provisions." The certificate holder isn't promised a notice. See [how to find out when a policy is canceled](/blog/notice-of-cancellation-coi/).

### What are the most common gaps on a contractor COI?

The most common contractor COI gaps look fine on a quick read. Anyone who knows how to read a certificate of insurance checks the same five places every time.

1. **Umbrella or excess below the requirement.** Project requirements often ask for more than a trade contractor carries on its standard program.
2. **Additional insured that stops when the job does.** CG 20 10 covers ongoing operations. You need completed operations too, usually CG 20 37 or a blanket form that includes it. See [completed operations additional insured](/blog/completed-operations-additional-insured/).
3. **An aggregate shared across every job.** When the "applies per" box says policy, one bad claim elsewhere can empty it. The fix is a designated construction project aggregate endorsement, which [IRMI defines](https://www.irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions/designated-construction-project-general-aggregate-limit-endorsement). See [per project aggregate](/blog/per-project-aggregate-coi/).
4. **A named insured that doesn't match the contract.** The wrong entity on the certificate means you can't be sure the right one is covered.
5. **Missing waiver or primary wording.** A checked SUBR WVD box isn't a waiver. Ask for the [waiver of subrogation endorsement](/blog/waiver-of-subrogation-coi/) and the [primary and noncontributory endorsement](/blog/primary-and-noncontributory/).

### How do state rules change what you check on a certificate of insurance?

State rules change which certificate of insurance lines you can rely on. Workers' compensation thresholds, monopolistic workers' comp states, license insurance minimums and anti-indemnity statutes that limit additional insured requirements all vary. Check the [contractor COI requirements for your state](/coi-requirements/) before you write the project requirements for limits or endorsements on a job there.

### How do you get a gap on a contractor COI fixed?

You get a gap on a contractor COI fixed by asking the contractor's broker for one specific change. The review checklist from [ISO](https://amtrustfinancial.com/getmedia/35303f0c-4a43-449b-bcb0-0fd07c75b947/Reviewing-Certificates-of-Insurance.pdf) gives the same advice: put the deficiency in writing and get a corrected certificate before work starts. A short note works best:

> Hi, for the Main Street project our project requirements call for umbrella limits of $5 million each occurrence and additional insured coverage for completed operations. The certificate dated October 2 shows $2 million umbrella and CG 20 10 only. Can you send an updated certificate and the CG 20 37 or equivalent endorsement?

Specific asks get fixed in days. Vague ones ("please send an updated COI") come back with the same certificate. And a review is only as good as its date, so recheck at every renewal and before every expiration on the job. Knowing how to read a certificate of insurance once isn't the same as knowing the contractor is covered today. [Run a free COI risk check](/#demo) on one project to see what a full review finds.

### Common questions

#### How do you read a certificate of insurance?

Read it top to bottom against your project requirements: the named insured, the insurers, each coverage line with its policy number, dates and limits, the ADDL INSD and SUBR WVD columns, the description of operations and the certificate holder. Then ask for the endorsement forms the checked boxes point to, because the certificate itself confers no rights.

#### What should I look for on a contractor's certificate of insurance?

Check that the named insured matches the contracting entity, that every required coverage is listed with limits at or above the project requirements, that the policy dates cover the work, that required endorsements are referenced and provided, and that the certificate holder and description of operations are correct for this project.

#### What are the most common contractor COI gaps?

The most common contractor COI gaps are umbrella or excess limits below the requirement, additional insured coverage that leaves out completed operations, a general aggregate that isn't per project, a named insured that doesn't match the contract, and policies that expire before the work ends. Each one looks fine on a quick scan of the certificate.

#### Does a checked additional insured box mean I'm covered?

No. The ACORD 25 says that if the certificate holder is an additional insured, the policy must have additional insured provisions or be endorsed, and that a statement on the certificate doesn't replace the endorsement. Ask for the endorsement form and check that it covers both ongoing and completed operations when your contract requires it.

#### Do the limits on a certificate of insurance show the full policy limits?

Not always. The 2025/12 ACORD 25 says the limits shown include amounts requested by the certificate holder and may not reflect policy limits above those requested, and that they may have been reduced by paid claims. Treat the limits as a floor that meets your requirement, not a full picture of the policy.

#### Who fixes a gap on a contractor COI?

The contractor's insurance broker or agent fixes it. The fastest path is to send the broker the specific requirement that isn't met, quoted from your project requirements, plus the line on the certificate or endorsement that falls short, so they can endorse the policy or issue a corrected certificate in one pass.

4. [Designated construction project general aggregate limit endorsement (definition)](https://www.irmi.com/term/insurance-definitions/designated-construction-project-general-aggregate-limit-endorsement), IRMI

## 3 takeaways from day 1 of IRMI's Construction Risk Conference

> Margins are thin, umbrella is where the pain is, and underwriters are starting to ask how contractors manage the trades they hire.

Published Oct 27, 2026 by Forsured. Event takeaways. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-crc-2026-day-1-takeaways/

![12 to 16: Bids on jobs that once drew 2 to 4, per ABC chief economist Anirban Basu](https://forsured.ai/blog/irmi-crc-2026-day-1-takeaways/hero.png)

### The short version

- Bids are crowded: ABC chief economist Anirban Basu says jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids now draw as many as 12 to 16, and about a third of contractors expect margins to shrink.
- WTW expects umbrella and excess rates to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, and brokers want renewal data on how often contracts demand high umbrella limits.
- Carriers give favorable consideration to strong management of the contractors a firm hires, so contractor COI compliance is becoming an underwriting story.

Day 1 at IRMI's Construction Risk Conference in National Harbor is in the books. Here are the three things that stuck with us from Monday, and what each one means for anyone collecting contractor COIs.

### 1. Margins are thin, and bids are crowded

Anirban Basu, chief economist at Associated Builders and Contractors, opened CRC's Monday general session. His recent numbers, reported by Construction Dive, set the tone: projects that once drew two to four bids are now drawing as many as 12 to 16, and about 32% of contractors surveyed expect profit margins to decline over the next year, up from 26% in July.

When the low bid wins, a contractor's insurance gap isn't a paperwork problem. It's a margin problem. A trade contractor that trimmed its umbrella to sharpen a number is the one whose gap lands back on the GC's program after a loss.

### 2. Umbrella is where the pain is

WTW expects umbrella and excess rates for construction to rise another 5% to 15% in 2027, the same range it gives auto liability, while general liability runs flat to up 10%.

A broker we sat down with asked for something simple: show me how many of last year's contracts required a high umbrella limit, so I can walk into renewal with data instead of guesses. That data exists in every GC's contractor COI file. It just isn't searchable when the certificates are PDFs in an inbox.

### 3. Contractor management is becoming an underwriting factor

WTW's outlook says carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to firms with strong management of the trades they hire, alongside loss experience and fleet controls. "When Compliance Isn't Coverage" was on Monday's agenda for a reason: a contractor COI in a file isn't proof of coverage, and underwriters know it.

For a GC, that turns COI review from back-office cleanup into something you can show a carrier at renewal: every contractor checked against project requirements, every gap tracked to a fix.

Want to see what your own contractor COI file would tell a carrier? That's what our free COI risk check is for.

## What the 2027 construction insurance outlook means for contractor COIs

> Umbrella and excess keep climbing while most other lines hold steady. That's exactly the line where contractors are most likely to fall short of project requirements.

Published Oct 26, 2026 by Forsured. Market outlook. Source: https://forsured.ai/blog/construction-insurance-2027-renewal-outlook/

![+5% to 15%: Forecast 2027 rate change for construction umbrella and excess liability](https://forsured.ai/blog/construction-insurance-2027-renewal-outlook/hero.png)

### The short version

- WTW's 2027 outlook for construction: umbrella and excess up 5% to 15%, auto up 5% to 15%, general liability flat to up 10%, workers' compensation flat to up 5%.
- Lead umbrella and excess on wrap-up programs (OCIPs and CCIPs) is also expected up 5% to 15%.
- When umbrella costs rise, trade contractors are tempted to carry less than project requirements demand, so umbrella is the line to check first on every contractor COI.
- Carriers favor firms with strong management of the contractors they hire, which makes a clean contractor COI record useful at renewal.

WTW published its Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027 report for construction on October 1. The headline for anyone managing contractor COIs: most lines are steady, and the expensive one keeps getting more expensive.

### The outlook by line

| Coverage | WTW 2027 forecast |
| --- | --- |
| Umbrella and excess liability | Up 5% to 15% |
| Auto liability | Up 5% to 15% |
| General liability | Flat to up 10% |
| Workers' compensation | Flat to up 5% |
| Project-specific builders risk (non-high hazard) | Down 2.5% to up 2.5% |
| Master builders risk | Down 5% to up 5% |
| Contractor's professional liability (annual) | Flat to up 5% |
| Wrap-ups (OCIP and CCIP), lead umbrella and excess | Up 5% to 15% |

### Umbrella has been the pressure point for years

This isn't new. Back in 2021, ENR reported that umbrella and excess renewals were costing contractors 50% to 100% more, as carriers raised prices, cut limits and raised attachment points. Rates have cooled since then, but umbrella keeps rising faster than the rest of the program.

### Why that shows up in your contractor COIs

Project requirements rarely bend to the market. If the contract calls for a $10 million umbrella, it calls for $10 million whether the trade contractor's renewal went up 5% or 15%.

Put that next to a bidding market where, as Construction Dive reported from ABC's Anirban Basu, jobs that once drew 2 to 4 bids are drawing 12 to 16. Thin margins and rising umbrella costs push in the same direction: carry less, and hope nobody checks.

So check umbrella first. On every contractor COI, confirm the umbrella or excess limit meets the project requirement, that it follows form over the underlying policies the contract requires, and that it won't expire before the work is done.

### The upside at your own renewal

WTW notes that carriers give favorable underwriting consideration to strong management of the trades a firm hires. A record showing every contractor checked against project requirements, with each gap tracked to a fix, is the kind of evidence an underwriter can use. A folder of unread certificates isn't.

WTW's Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027 report forecasts umbrella and excess liability rates for construction up 5% to 15%.

WTW expects builders risk to be roughly flat (minus 2.5% to plus 2.5% for non-high hazard project-specific builders risk), workers' compensation flat to up 5%, and contractor's professional liability flat to up 5% on annual programs.
